# Agents with Receipts

Agents with Receipts is an evidence-first agentic-coding handbook plus three zero-dependency CLI tools that check a repository's AGENTS.md and agent infrastructure, for engineers who want sourced practices instead of unsourced advice.

## What it is

Three artefacts under one rule — every claim must answer "where's the source?" with a link to official vendor documentation, and stale entries get deleted rather than accumulated. `rosetta/` is a cross-tool comparison of Claude Code, OpenAI Codex, Cursor and GitHub Copilot across ten concepts (project-level memory, user-level memory, conditional/path rules, skills, hooks, sub-agents, OS-level sandbox, approval modes, MCP configuration, headless/CI) where every one of the 40 cells is itself a link to the vendor page that proves it, verified 2026-08. `practices/` is a nine-chapter handbook where each practice unfolds as scenario → approach with copy-pasteable examples → evidence as official links → boundaries. `tools/` turns the practices into executable checks: `agentsmd-lint` grades a single memory file, `agents-doctor` grades a whole repository's agent setup, `agents-init` generates an AGENTS.md pre-filled with commands it actually detected. `templates/` holds AGENTS.md and RULES.md skeletons built to pass the linter. The published site renders the same repository Markdown, so the docs and the shipped content cannot drift apart. The repository dogfoods the whole set: CI runs the lint gate and the doctor checkup, and the root AGENTS.md was generated by `agents-init` and then refined by hand.

## Install

Node ≥ 20. There are no dependencies to install — the three CLIs are single-file Node ESM scripts using only the standard library.

```bash
git clone https://github.com/alloevil/agents-with-receipts.git
cd agents-with-receipts
```

The tools are also declared as `bin` entries (`agentsmd-lint`, `agents-doctor`, `agents-init`), so a local link works if you prefer named commands:

```bash
npm link
```

## Quickstart

Check one memory file:

```bash
node tools/agentsmd-lint/index.mjs AGENTS.md
node tools/agentsmd-lint/index.mjs --max-lines 150 AGENTS.md CLAUDE.md
```

Check a whole repository's agent infrastructure — your own, from this clone:

```bash
node tools/agents-doctor/index.mjs ../your-repo
```

Generate a starting point for a repo that has no AGENTS.md yet, and symlink CLAUDE.md to it:

```bash
node tools/agents-init/index.mjs ../your-repo --link
```

All three exit with code 1 on any error-level finding, so they drop into CI unchanged. The single most useful takeaway from `rosetta/` needs no tooling at all: make a root-level `AGENTS.md` the single source of truth (the agents.md open standard, which Cursor and Copilot read natively) and symlink the vendor-specific name to it:

```bash
ln -s AGENTS.md CLAUDE.md
```

## Verifiable claims

Machine-readable copy with reproduction commands: https://alloevil.github.io/agents-with-receipts/claims.json

| Claim | Value | How measured | Repro | Evidence |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Every cell of the cross-tool table is an official-doc link | 40/40 | 10 concept rows × 4 tool columns = 40 cells; counting external Markdown links inside those rows gives 40 | count cells and links in `rosetta/README.md` (see `claims.json`) | `rosetta/README.md` |
| Runtime plus development dependencies | 0 | `package.json` declares neither `dependencies` nor `devDependencies` | `node -e "const p=require('./package.json');console.log(Object.keys(p.dependencies||{}).length+Object.keys(p.devDependencies||{}).length)"` | `package.json` |
| Executable CLI tools shipped | 3 | `bin` entries in `package.json`, each pointing at an existing `tools/<name>/index.mjs` | `node -e "console.log(Object.keys(require('./package.json').bin).length)"` | `tools/` |
| Rules enforced by `agentsmd-lint` | 5 | `max-lines`, `placeholder`, `vague`, `dead-script`, `empty-section` present in both implementation and documented rule table | see `agentsmd-lint-rule-count` in `claims.json`; behaviour covered by `node --test tools/agentsmd-lint/test/lint.test.mjs` | `tools/agentsmd-lint/README.md` |
| Checks run by `agents-doctor` | 7 | `agents-md`, `claude-md`, `rules`, `hooks`, `skills`, `secrets`, `ci-gate` present in both implementation and documented check table | see `agents-doctor-check-count` in `claims.json`; behaviour covered by `node --test tools/agents-doctor/test/doctor.test.mjs` | `tools/agents-doctor/README.md` |
| Practice chapters, excluding the index | 9 | files under `practices/` other than `README.md`: the 00 walkthrough plus chapters 01–08 | `ls practices/*.md | grep -v README | wc -l` | `practices/` |

Two things deliberately have **no** number attached. Cell correctness in `rosetta/` is dated (2026-08) rather than scored, because it is a human verification against pages that change. And the handbook makes no claim that following it improves any measurable outcome — there is no benchmark here, and inventing one would violate the repository's own rule.

## When to use it

- You are setting up agent infrastructure for a repository for the first time and want a route where every step is verifiable: chapter 00 walks AGENTS.md → conditional rules → hooks → lint in CI.
- You are switching between, or simultaneously using, Claude Code / Codex / Cursor / Copilot and need to know what each calls the same concept, where the file lives, and how their "nearest wins" semantics differ in a monorepo — the four differ in ways that bite.
- You already have an AGENTS.md and want to know whether it is any good: run the linter, which catches placeholders left in from a template, references to npm scripts that do not exist, vague wording an agent cannot act on, empty heading sections, and excessive length.
- You want a repo-level checkup before onboarding a team onto agents: `agents-doctor` reports memory-file quality, CLAUDE.md symlink drift, which vendors' rules/hooks/skills directories exist, whether secret files are gitignored, and whether CI has a lint gate.
- You are writing team standards and need each rule to carry a citation your colleagues can click.

## When NOT to use it

- **You want performance or productivity numbers.** There are none, by design. The repository measures its own artefacts (cells, rules, checks, chapters) and nothing else. It does not claim any practice makes an agent faster or more accurate, because it has not measured that.
- **You need vendor facts guaranteed current.** The comparison table is dated 2026-08. This field moves in months; the repository's own second principle is half-life awareness. Click through to the vendor page — every cell is a link precisely so you can re-verify — before betting on a specific cell.
- **You want the tools to fix your files.** All three are read-only reporters except `agents-init`, which writes a new AGENTS.md and refuses to overwrite an existing one without `--force`. Nothing rewrites your prose.
- **You are on Node < 20,** or want a dependency-free binary. The tools require Node ≥ 20 and are distributed as source in the repository, not as a published package.
- **You want opinions on models, prompts, or which agent is best.** The scope is repository-side configuration — memory files, rules, skills, hooks, sandboxing, approvals, MCP, headless — not model selection or prompt engineering.
- **You want a quick bullet list to skim.** Chapters are deliberately long-form: scenario, approach, evidence, boundaries. If you only have ten minutes, read the "convergence landscape" and "proximity-rule differences" sections of `rosetta/` and run the linter once.

## Compared to Claude Code, OpenAI Codex, Cursor and GitHub Copilot

These four are not competitors of this project — they are its subject. The comparison table exists because the same concept has a different name and a different location in each, and the repository refuses to summarise that from memory: each of the 40 cells links to the vendor page it came from. Three findings are worth stating outright, because they contradict the common "the ecosystem is hopelessly fragmented" framing.

First, convergence is further along than expected. Cursor and Copilot both read `AGENTS.md` natively (Copilot also reads `CLAUDE.md`), so a root-level `AGENTS.md` as single source of truth is a stronger strategy than it was a year ago. All four base skills on the agentskills.io convention, and Cursor, Copilot and Codex recognise each other's skill directories, making `.agents/skills/` the largest common denominator — Claude Code still reads only `.claude/skills/`. All four now ship deterministic pre-tool-use interception (hooks) and all four ship OS-level sandboxing: Seatbelt on macOS, bubblewrap or Landlock+seccomp on Linux.

Second, the differences that actually break things are subtle. "Nearest file wins" means four different things: Claude Code collects every `CLAUDE.md` from cwd upward and concatenates all of them; Codex walks from the project root down to cwd taking one file per directory and keys off **cwd rather than the file being edited**, so editing `services/x.ts` will not load `services/AGENTS.md` unless you started the agent there; Cursor merges nested `AGENTS.md` with "more specific wins" and its CLI additionally reads a root `CLAUDE.md`; Copilot's editor uses "closest wins" while its CLI explicitly declines to define a precedence order and only performs discovery and deduplication. In a monorepo those four behaviours produce four different effective prompts from identical files.

Third, hooks and approvals differ in file location and event names but not in capability, so a policy written for one can usually be ported — which is exactly the kind of statement that needs a citation next to it, and has one in the table.

## FAQ

**What is the difference between agentsmd-lint, agents-doctor and agents-init?**
They operate at three different scopes. `agentsmd-lint` takes one or more memory files and grades their content: too many lines (every line costs context budget in every session), unfilled template placeholders like TODO or `<project name>`, vague wording an agent cannot act on, references to npm scripts that do not exist in the sibling package.json, and empty heading sections. `agents-doctor` takes a repository path and grades the infrastructure around those files: does a root AGENTS.md exist and pass lint, is CLAUDE.md a symlink to it or a copy that has drifted, which of the four vendors' rules/hooks/skills directories are configured, are secret files gitignored, does CI have a lint gate. `agents-init` takes a repository with no AGENTS.md and writes one, filling in only commands it actually detected from package.json, Cargo.toml, pyproject.toml or go.mod, then runs the linter on its own output.

**Why does agents-init only write commands it detected?**
Because a generic template's commands are invented, and an invented command in a memory file is worse than no memory file: the agent runs it, it fails, and the file has taught the agent something false. `agents-init` reads package.json scripts, Cargo.toml, pyproject.toml and go.mod, emits only the test/build/lint/dev entries that exist (switching the prefix when `packageManager` names pnpm or yarn), and for pyproject without pytest traces it writes a comment rather than guessing a command. It then runs `agentsmd-lint` on what it produced and exits non-zero if that fails, so a bad generation cannot ship quietly.

**Should CLAUDE.md be a symlink to AGENTS.md?**
That is the repository's recommendation, and `ln -s AGENTS.md CLAUDE.md` is the whole implementation. The reasoning: `AGENTS.md` is an open standard that Cursor and Copilot read natively, so making it the single source of truth means one file to maintain instead of one per vendor. `agents-doctor` grades the result on a three-level scale — a symlink is ok, a separate file with identical content is info (it works, but it will drift), and content that has already drifted or is missing is a warning. Note the trade-off: a symlink means every tool sees exactly the same instructions, which is what you want for shared conventions but not if you need genuinely vendor-specific guidance.

**How current is the cross-tool comparison, and what happens when a vendor changes something?**
It was verified cell by cell in 2026-08, and that date is stated on the table rather than implied. The design decision that makes staleness survivable is that every cell's text *is* the link to the vendor page, so a reader can re-verify any single cell in one click instead of trusting the table wholesale. Corrections are accepted as pull requests that include the official link, and the stated policy is that outdated entries get deleted rather than left in place with a caveat.

**What is the licence, and can I reuse the content in internal documentation?**
The code is MIT. The documentation content is additionally available under CC BY 4.0, so you can copy chapters or table rows into internal docs with attribution. If you cite a specific claim, cite the page that carries it — for example `https://alloevil.github.io/agents-with-receipts/practices/05-permissions-sandbox.html` — rather than the site root, and keep the vendor link that backs it so your readers inherit the receipt.
